article.title: COINTELPRO: The FBI's Secret War on Black Liberation—and the Injustice That Never Ended
article.author: Sharon Kyle
article.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. In 1971, eight ordinary Americans did something extraordinary. They broke into an FBI office in Media, Pennsylvania, and stole government documents exposing a secret campaign against American citizens exercising their constitutional rights. Their actions helped expose what would become one of the most notorious domestic intelligence scandals in American history: COINTELPRO, the FBI's Counterintelligence Program. But exposing government wrongdoing and obtaining justice for its victims are two entirely different things. More than four decades later, I moderated a discussion at Occidental College that brought together people who had exposed the FBI's secret operations and Black activists who had experienced the consequences of government repression firsthand. The panel included Bonnie Raines, one of the eight activists responsible for the historic FBI burglary; Betty Medsger, the former Washington Post journalist who helped bring the stolen documents to public attention; and former Black Panthers Harold Taylor and Hank Jones, whose experiences revealed how the government's pursuit of Black liberation activists continued long after COINTELPRO was officially discontinued. The event, part of the Courage and Resistance Tour, took place in 2015. Their stories raised questions that remain relevant today: What happens when government agencies use their enormous investigative powers to suppress political dissent? Who holds those agencies accountable? And what remedies are available to the people whose lives have been destroyed? Eight Ordinary Americans Take on the FBI On March 8, 1971, millions of Americans were watching Muhammad Ali fight Joe Frazier in what had been promoted as the Fight of the Century. In Media, Pennsylvania, eight antiwar activists were carrying out a very different kind of confrontation. Calling themselves the Citizens' Commission to Investigate the FBI, they entered a small FBI office and removed approximately 1,000 documents. They weren't looking for money. They were looking for evidence. For years, organizers opposing the Vietnam War suspected that the government was infiltrating their organizations, monitoring their activities, and working to undermine their effectiveness. They believed the FBI was violating the constitutional rights of Americans who were doing little more than challenging their government's policies. But they couldn't prove it. Bonnie Raines, then 29 and the mother of three young children, was among the eight. During our discussion, she explained how the group moved from conventional protest to what she described as nonviolent disruption. They had marched, circulated petitions, attended demonstrations, and traveled to Washington. Nevertheless, the Vietnam War continued, and the government's attempts to suppress opposition appeared to intensify. Their group decided that exposing FBI misconduct required something more. Bonnie visited the FBI office while pretending to be a college student interested in employment opportunities for women. Her assignment was to determine whether the office had security measures that would prevent the burglary. It did not. The activists chose the night of the Ali-Frazier fight, believing that the event would distract police and residents of the building. They escaped without detection. The FBI launched an extensive investigation but never apprehended the burglars. Their identities remained secret for more than four decades. A Journalist Receives the Evidence On March 23, 1971, Betty Medsger arrived at her Washington Post office and discovered an unusual envelope among her correspondence. It contained copies of documents from the burglarized FBI office. One of the records instructed FBI agents to create an atmosphere that would "enhance the paranoia" among political activists, encouraging them to believe government agents might be watching everywhere. Other documents described informants planted in political organizations, surveillance of college campuses, and extensive monitoring of Black communities. The documents had also been sent to other journalists and two members of Congress. But those recipients did not immediately publish the revelations. The congressional recipients turned the materials over to the FBI. At the Los Angeles Times, the documents were intercepted before reaching the intended reporter. The New York Times initially declined to publish its copy. Medsger and The Washington Post took a different approach. Despite pressure from federal officials, the newspaper published the findings, exposing practices that the FBI had concealed from the American people. The disclosures eventually helped expose COINTELPRO and contributed to congressional investigations into abuses by the nation's intelligence agencies. Medsger later documented the complete story in her book, The Burglary: The Discovery of J. Edgar Hoover's Secret FBI . What she discovered was not simply an intelligence agency collecting information. It was an agency actively interfering with the political activities of people whose views its director opposed. When Being Black Was Enough to Attract FBI Surveillance One of the most disturbing revelations concerned the surveillance of African Americans. During our panel discussion, Medsger explained that documents from the FBI office revealed surveillance directed at Black students at Swarthmore College. These students were not necessarily suspected of committing crimes. Their racial identity was sufficient to attract government attention. Other FBI records described informant networks monitoring Black communities in churches, libraries, restaurants, schools, and neighborhood gathering places. The Bureau was treating ordinary Black life as a potential security concern. That distinction matters because racial profiling is not merely an unfortunate consequence of aggressive law enforcement. It is a mechanism through which government power can reinforce an existing racial hierarchy. When an entire population is treated as inherently suspicious, the constitutional promise of equal protection becomes profoundly unequal in practice. And the FBI's campaign against the Black Panther Party demonstrated just how destructive that inequality could become. COINTELPRO and the Destruction of Black Political Organizing COINTELPRO began in 1956, initially targeting the Communist Party. Its operations eventually expanded to include other political organizations, civil rights activists, antiwar groups, and Black liberation movements. The Black Panther Party became a major target in 1967. The FBI used informants, anonymous letters, disinformation, infiltration, and efforts to provoke internal conflict. The objective was not simply to gather intelligence about possible criminal activity. It was also to disrupt organizations and undermine their political influence. Martin Luther King Jr. was subjected to extensive FBI surveillance and attempts to discredit him. The Black Panthers faced an especially aggressive campaign. Government efforts to portray the Panthers primarily as violent extremists obscured their extensive community organizing. The party established free breakfast programs for children, health initiatives, political education programs, and other community services. These activities challenged public institutions that had failed to meet the needs of Black communities. Harold Taylor explained why he had joined the Black Panther Party as a young man in South Los Angeles. He wanted to defend his community and help improve the conditions under which its members lived. His commitment was not to violence for its own sake, but to community protection and self-determination. That commitment placed him in the path of government repression. Harold Taylor: Torture and Coerced Confessions During our interview, Taylor described an encounter with Los Angeles police in the early 1970s that ended with officers firing repeatedly into the car in which he was riding. He was shot multiple times. Taylor subsequently faced criminal charges arising from the confrontation. He told our audience that a jury ultimately found he had acted in self-defense. But his ordeal did not end there. After leaving California, Taylor was arrested in New Orleans, where he described being subjected to severe physical and psychological abuse during police interrogations. He recounted beatings, sleep deprivation, denial of food and water, suffocation with plastic bags, electric shocks, and simulated drowning. The purpose, he said, was to force statements implicating other Black Panthers in criminal activity. Taylor described holding out for days before finally agreeing to make statements dictated by his interrogators. He also recounted being brought before a judge, only to be returned to the custody of officers he accused of torturing him. His account was horrifying. But equally disturbing was the role those statements would play in later efforts to prosecute former Black Panthers. The case involved the 1971 killing of San Francisco police officer John V. Young during an attack on the Ingleside Police Station. Statements obtained during the New Orleans interrogations became part of the investigation. The defendants and their supporters maintained that those statements were the product of torture and could not be trusted. The allegations of coercion helped undermine the earlier prosecutions. Yet, decades later, the same historical case would return. The San Francisco 8: When the Government Reopened the Past Following the terrorist attacks of September 11, 2001, the federal government substantially expanded its national-security apparatus. Congress enacted the USA PATRIOT Act. The Department of Homeland Security was created. Federal and local law enforcement agencies increased cooperation through counterterrorism investigations. Within this atmosphere, authorities revisited investigations involving former Black Panthers. In 2003, investigators approached Hank Jones at his home. Jones told our audience that the officers questioned him about his former political associations, including the Black Panther Party and the Weather Underground. One investigator, Jones recalled, remarked on his home and warned that he could lose everything if he failed to cooperate. Jones described the encounter as an unmistakable threat. Investigators eventually obtained legal process compelling him to appear before a grand jury. The renewed investigation would become known as the San Francisco 8 case. In January 2007, California authorities brought charges against eight men in connection with the 1971 killing of Officer Young. They were Herman Bell, Jalil Muntaqim, Harold Taylor, Hank Jones, Ray Boudreaux, Richard Brown, Richard O'Neal, and Francisco Torres. Several had been under investigation decades earlier, and the renewed case raised questions about evidence associated with the original New Orleans interrogations. Defense supporters argued that the prosecution represented a continuation of the government's historical campaign against Black liberation organizations. Prosecutors maintained that they were seeking accountability for an unsolved police killing. But the defendants faced an enormous personal burden. By 2007, many were older men who had spent decades raising families, working, and contributing to their communities. Now they faced serious criminal charges carrying the possibility of spending the remainder of their lives in prison. Their families faced renewed uncertainty. The men endured repeated court appearances, restrictions on their lives, and years of defending themselves against accusations arising from events nearly four decades earlier. Legal representation became a major undertaking involving defense attorneys, investigators, expert witnesses, and a nationwide network of supporters. Community organizations mobilized to raise awareness and provide assistance. The financial burden extended beyond courtroom expenses. The proceedings disrupted ordinary employment, family life, travel, and the stability the defendants had built over decades. And the case did not simply end with everyone being acquitted. In 2008, prosecutors dismissed the charges against Richard O'Neal. The remaining defendants became known as the San Francisco 7. In 2009, Herman Bell entered a guilty plea to a reduced charge of voluntary manslaughter, while Jalil Muntaqim entered a no-contest plea to a reduced conspiracy charge. Neither received additional prison time from the negotiated dispositions. As part of the broader resolution, prosecutors dismissed charges against Hank Jones, Harold Taylor, Ray Boudreaux, and Richard Brown, acknowledging that they lacked sufficient evidence to proceed. Francisco Torres continued fighting the remaining charges until August 2011, when his case was dismissed. For Jones and Taylor, the dismissals ended the immediate threat of conviction. But what did they restore? They did not return the years spent defending against prosecution. They did not compensate the men for the disruption of their lives or the psychological strain on their families. And they did not resolve the larger question of accountability for the original allegations of torture. The San Francisco 8 case demonstrated that legal proceedings can end without repairing the damage they have caused. The dismissal of a prosecution is not the same as restoration of the life disrupted by that prosecution. The Remedies That Never Came The exposure of COINTELPRO produced important institutional changes. Congress investigated intelligence abuses through the Church Committee. New guidelines attempted to restrict domestic intelligence operations. Oversight mechanisms were strengthened. But what happened to the people whose rights had already been violated? Some victims obtained financial settlements through civil litigation. The families and survivors of Black Panther leaders Fred Hampton and Mark Clark, killed during a 1969 Chicago police raid, reached a $1.85 million settlement in 1983. Geronimo ji Jaga Pratt, a former Black Panther who spent approximately 25 years imprisoned following a murder conviction that was eventually overturned, obtained a $4.5 million settlement in 2000. Other victims secured the dismissal of charges, access to FBI records, or favorable civil judgments. But the government never established a comprehensive national reparations process for COINTELPRO victims. There was no systematic effort to identify everyone targeted, determine the harm they suffered, compensate their losses, or review every criminal conviction potentially affected by illegal government conduct. Nor was there a comprehensive criminal reckoning for officials who directed or participated in COINTELPRO's abuses. This distinction is central to understanding the limitations of American institutional reform. Government agencies may revise their policies, adopt new procedures, and promise improved oversight without taking responsibility for the damage already inflicted. Institutional reform is not the same as justice for victims. And reform without accountability can leave the structures that permitted abuse substantially intact. The Surveillance State Did Not Disappear The 2015 Occidental College discussion opened with an ACLU presentation concerning contemporary law enforcement surveillance. The ACLU described local agencies acquiring drones, automated license plate readers, and cell-site simulators, sometimes without meaningful public debate or adequate oversight. Its representative warned that surveillance technologies purchased for narrowly defined purposes could later be used much more broadly. The organization advocated ordinances requiring public disclosure, approval by elected officials, clearly defined policies, and mechanisms for accountability. The technology available to government agencies today bears little resemblance to the paper files and telephone informants of Hoover's era. Modern surveillance can collect, aggregate, and analyze enormous quantities of information. But the fundamental constitutional questions remain. Who decides which people or communities will be monitored? What evidence is required before surveillance begins? Who supervises the agencies conducting it? What remedies exist when surveillance becomes a tool of political repression? And who pays the price when government officials abuse their authority? These are not merely questions about technology. They are questions about the distribution of power in a democracy. Exposure Is Not Justice One of the most powerful aspects of our discussion was the contrast between the experiences of those who exposed FBI misconduct and the Black activists who experienced some of its harshest consequences. Bonnie Raines and her fellow activists risked imprisonment to obtain evidence of government wrongdoing. Their courage deserves recognition. But the experiences of Harold Taylor and Hank Jones demonstrate that Black activists challenging entrenched power faced consequences extending far beyond surveillance. For some, those consequences included violence, torture, wrongful imprisonment, damaged relationships, and decades of uncertainty. Even after COINTELPRO became a national scandal, the men who would become the San Francisco 8 found themselves once again confronting the machinery of criminal prosecution. The government had changed its rules. The people who had been targeted were still living with the consequences. That contrast raises a profound question about the meaning of democracy. A constitutional guarantee is meaningful only to the extent that people can exercise it without facing unlawful retaliation. And government accountability is meaningful only when those responsible for abuses face consequences and the people harmed receive genuine remedies. Near the conclusion of our discussion, the panelists urged the audience to organize, question authority, support political prisoners, and demand more meaningful oversight. Their message was not that resistance is easy or that victories are inevitable. It was that public pressure, collective action, and independent journalism can expose wrongdoing that powerful institutions would otherwise conceal. The 1971 FBI burglary demonstrated that ordinary citizens could challenge one of the most powerful law enforcement agencies in the country. The experiences of Taylor and Jones demonstrated that exposing injustice is not enough. Until the people harmed by government repression receive meaningful remedies—and the institutions responsible are held accountable—the struggle for justice remains unfinished.
